scenes.tts: Most sensory receptors are excited by their stimulus. Rods and cones are turned down by theirs. How does quieting a cell let you see?
scenes.visual: Title card: One Cell Counts. A hair cell and a touch ending light up when stimulated; beside them a rod dims as a flash hits it. Question on screen: how does quieting a cell let you see?
scenes.narration: Most sensory receptors are excited by their stimulus. Rods and cones are turned down by theirs. How does quieting a cell let you see?

scenes.tts: Start with a rod in the dark. Cyclic G M P holds channels open in its outer segment.
scenes.caption: Start with a rod in the dark. cGMP holds channels open in its outer segment.
scenes.visual: A rod drawn upright: outer segment at top, inner segment, terminal at the bottom. Small cGMP dots hold channel pores open in the outer segment. Label: CNG channels, held open by cGMP.
scenes.narration: Start with a rod in the dark. cGMP holds channels open in its outer segment.

scenes.tts: Sodium and calcium flow in. This steady dark current keeps the rod depolarized, releasing glutamate all the time.
scenes.visual: Sodium and calcium ions stream in at the outer segment; an arrow loop shows current flowing in at the outer segment and out at the inner segment. Vesicles release steadily at the terminal. Label: dark current.
scenes.narration: Sodium and calcium flow in. This steady dark current keeps the rod depolarized, releasing glutamate all the time.

scenes.tts: Potassium channels in the inner segment pull the other way. You have seen this tug of war before.
scenes.visual: Beside the rod, the voltage scale from the Action Potential films: E_K (about −80 mV) on the left, 0 mV on the right, a marker between. One rope pulls toward 0 mV (CNG channels), one toward E_K (potassium channels).
scenes.narration: Potassium channels in the inner segment pull the other way. You have seen this tug of war before.

scenes.tts: With the two pulls about equal, the voltage settles in between, near minus forty millivolts.
scenes.caption: With the two pulls about equal, the voltage settles in between, near −40 mV.
scenes.visual: The two ropes balance; the marker settles at about −40 mV. Label: dark potential, about −40 mV (simple two-conductance sketch).
scenes.narration: With the two pulls about equal, the voltage settles in between, near −40 mV.

scenes.tts: Now a photon arrives. It straightens the retinal inside rhodopsin, and the pigment becomes active.
scenes.visual: A photon strikes a disc in the outer segment. Inside a rhodopsin molecule the bent retinal straightens. Labels: 11-cis to all-trans retinal; rhodopsin active.
scenes.narration: Now a photon arrives. It straightens the retinal inside rhodopsin, and the pigment becomes active.

scenes.tts: One active rhodopsin switches on many transducins. That is where much of the gain, the amplification, comes from.
scenes.visual: A six-box chain appears along the bottom: photon, rhodopsin, transducin, PDE6, cGMP, CNG channels. The rhodopsin box lights, then fans out to many lit transducin icons. Label: gain.
scenes.narration: One active rhodopsin switches on many transducins. That is where much of the gain, the amplification, comes from.

scenes.tts: Transducin turns on an enzyme, P D E six, that destroys the messenger. The messenger falls, and the channels close.
scenes.visual: The chain lights in turn: PDE6 activates, cGMP dots disappear, channel pores shut one by one. Labels: PDE6; cGMP falls; CNG channels close.
scenes.narration: Transducin turns on an enzyme, PDE6, that destroys the messenger. The messenger falls, and the channels close.
scenes.caption: Transducin turns on an enzyme, PDE6, that destroys the messenger. The messenger falls, and the channels close.

scenes.tts: With fewer cation channels open, potassium wins the tug of war. The balance point slides toward potassium.
scenes.visual: The CNG rope slackens; the marker slides left toward E_K. Label: toward E_K.
scenes.narration: With fewer cation channels open, potassium wins the tug of war. The balance point slides toward potassium.

scenes.tts: The rod hyperpolarizes, and its glutamate release falls. Brighter light closes more channels. The response is graded.
scenes.visual: Vesicle release at the terminal slows. A brighter flash closes more channels and the marker slides farther. Labels: hyperpolarizes; less glutamate; graded, not all or none.
scenes.narration: The rod hyperpolarizes, and its glutamate release falls. Brighter light closes more channels. The response is graded.

scenes.tts: Calcium falls too: fewer open channels let less calcium in, while the rod keeps removing it. Low calcium speeds the remaking of the messenger. The rod recovers, and turns its gain down in brighter light.
scenes.visual: Fewer calcium dots enter as channels close, while calcium keeps leaving, so the dots thin out in the outer segment. A cyclase icon speeds up and cGMP dots return; some channels reopen and the marker drifts back. Labels: GCAPs stimulate the cyclase; recovery; light adaptation.
scenes.narration: Calcium falls too: fewer open channels let less calcium in, while the rod keeps removing it. Low calcium speeds the remaking of the messenger. The rod recovers, and turns its gain down in brighter light.

scenes.tts: How small can the signal be? Baylor, Lamb and Yau drew the outer segment of one toad rod into a glass pipette.
scenes.visual: A rod outer segment drawn into the snug tip of a glass pipette. Label: suction electrode, toad rod (Baylor, Lamb and Yau, 1979). A flat current trace starts beside it.
scenes.narration: How small can the signal be? Baylor, Lamb and Yau drew the outer segment of one toad rod into a glass pipette.

scenes.tts: They repeated a very dim flash many times. Some flashes gave nothing. Many gave a dip of about the same size, near one picoamp.
scenes.caption: They repeated a very dim flash many times. Some flashes gave nothing. Many gave a dip of about the same size, near 1 pA.
scenes.visual: The same dim flash repeated: trace after trace stacks up. Some flat, many with a dip of about the same size. Label: about 1 pA.
scenes.narration: They repeated a very dim flash many times. Some flashes gave nothing. Many gave a dip of about the same size, near 1 pA.

scenes.tts: The sizes did not vary smoothly. Each event was one pigment molecule, activated by one photon. In dim light, a rod counts photons.
scenes.visual: The dips drop into a histogram: one peak at zero, one near 1 pA, with some scatter around it. Label: one event = one photoisomerization. Caption on screen: a rod counts photons.
scenes.narration: The sizes did not vary smoothly. Each event was one pigment molecule, activated by one photon. In dim light, a rod counts photons.

scenes.tts: Two lights fall on one cone. One is dim, at the cone's best wavelength. One is brighter, far from it. Can the cone tell them apart?
scenes.visual: A cone with its broad sensitivity curve. A dim light at the curve's peak and a brighter light out on the curve's tail. Question on screen: can the cone tell them apart?
scenes.narration: Two lights fall on one cone. One is dim, at the cone's best wavelength. One is brighter, far from it. Can the cone tell them apart?

scenes.tts: Not if the two give it the same photon catch, with the same timing, under the same adaptation. Once absorbed, every photon has the same effect, whatever its wavelength.
scenes.visual: Both lights deliver the same mean catch of absorbed photons; a tag reads: same timing, same adaptation. The cone's mean graded traces match, with single trials scattering around them. Label: univariance.
scenes.narration: Not if the two give it the same photon catch, with the same timing, under the same adaptation. Once absorbed, every photon has the same effect, whatever its wavelength.

scenes.tts: So one photoreceptor cannot separate a change in wavelength from a change in intensity. The takeaway: one receptor is univariant; the circuit compares.
scenes.visual: The two matched lights give the same mean graded trace, under the same adaptation and timing. Label: univariance, wavelength and intensity cannot be told apart. Takeaway on screen: one receptor is univariant; the circuit compares.
scenes.narration: So one photoreceptor cannot separate a change in wavelength from a change in intensity. The takeaway: one receptor is univariant; the circuit compares.
